summary: Part II of Colmez and Nizioł's series on the cohomology of p-adic analytic spaces. It states analogues of Fontaine's C_dR and C_st conjectures for an arbitrary smooth dagger variety over C or over K - so with neither a properness nor a quasi-compactness nor a semistable-model hypothesis - and proves them for a large class of varieties. The statement in the de Rham-to-pro-etale direction (Conjecture 1.4 = Conjecture 6.21, the C_st-conjecture of the title) is that the fundamental diagram, whose corners are pro-etale cohomology H^i_proet(X,Q_p(r)), the Frobenius eigenspace (H^i_HK(X) (x) B^+_st)^{N=0,phi=p^r}, the r-th filtration step H^i(F^r RGamma_dR(X/B^+_dR)) and H^i_dR(X/B^+_dR), is bicartesian for i <= r, in the left heart of the derived category of convex Q_p-vector spaces. In the converse direction, Conjecture 1.6 recovers Hyodo-Kato and de Rham cohomology with Frobenius, monodromy and the Hodge filtration from the pro-etale cohomology of a variety over K, by taking G_K-equivariant homomorphisms into B_st and B_dR, and Conjecture 1.8 recovers them as modules, without those structures, over C. The main theorem is that all of this holds whenever X is small - meaning its B^+_dR-cohomology is free of finite rank - and has de Rham slopes >= 0, meaning each filtered (phi,N)-module (H^i_HK(X), F^0 H^i_dR(X/B_dR)) is acyclic; and that products of such varieties, analytifications of algebraic varieties and almost proper varieties are of this kind, as is a product of a proper and a Stein variety, by a limit argument. A second main theorem computes the height of pro-etale cohomology as the C-dimension of de Rham cohomology. The method is a geometrization: all four cohomologies are realized as quasi-Banach-Colmez spaces - the 'q' for quasi, because the finiteness conditions defining a Banach-Colmez space are relaxed to allow extensions by arbitrary torsion B^+_dR-modules - and the conjecture becomes the vanishing of the H^1 of a vector bundle on the Fargues-Fontaine curve, whence the four a priori different conjectures are all equivalent. The paper therefore needs, and builds, three bodies of theory before it reaches geometry: Fontaine's almost C-representations and the Hom-vanishing statements out of torsion B^+_dR-objects (Section 2); Banach-Colmez spaces via Le Bras's equivalence with a category of complexes of coherent sheaves on the curve, with curvature, the canonical filtration and a categorification of height as the rank of Hom_VS(-,B_dR) (Section 3); the category qBC of quasi-Banach-Colmez spaces, with a perfectoid computation of Ext^1_TVS(V_1,V_1) = C and a theorem that the module, Module and topological Hom and Ext all agree for reasonable objects (Section 4); and the notion of an acyclic filtered (phi,N,G_K)-module generalizing weak admissibility, with the computation of the Hom's out of a Frobenius eigenspace that drives the converse direction (Section 5).

items.name: Setup and conventions
items.statement: O_K is a complete discrete valuation ring with fraction field K of characteristic 0 and perfect residue field k of characteristic p, countable; K̄ an algebraic closure, O_K̄ the integral closure of O_K in it, C = K̂̄ the p-adic completion of K̄; W(k) = O_F with fraction field F, e = e_K the ramification index of K over F, F^nr the maximal unramified extension of F; G_K = Gal(K̄/K) and ϕ the absolute Frobenius of W(k); B_cris, B_st, B_dR are Fontaine's period rings, with B_dR = B^+_dR[1/t] and B_st = B^+_st[1/t]. O_K, O^×_K and O^0_K denote Spec(O_K) or Spf(O_K) with the trivial, the canonical (associated to the closed point) and the (N → O_K, 1 ↦ 0) log structure. Formal schemes are p-adic, locally of finite type and equidimensional; X_0 is the special fibre and X_n the reduction mod p^n. All rigid analytic spaces are over K or C and are assumed separated, taut and countable at infinity.

items.name: Conjecture 1.1: Fontaine's C_dR and C_st
items.statement: For X proper and smooth over K admitting a semistable model over O_K and i ≥ 0: (i) (C_dR) a functorial G_K-equivariant filtered isomorphism H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p) ⊗_{Q_p} B_dR ≅ H^i_dR(X) ⊗_K B_dR; (ii) (C_st) a functorial G_K-equivariant isomorphism commuting with ϕ and N, H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p) ⊗_{Q_p} B_st ≅ H^i_HK(X) ⊗_F B_st, compatible with the de Rham period morphism and with the inclusions B_st ⊂ B_dR and H^i_HK ⊂ H^i_dR.
items.note: Fontaine's conjectures, now theorems without the hypotheses of good models, properness or smoothness; the atlas owns the semistable comparison at CohomologyComparisons CP.4. This paper is the analytic analogue.

items.name: Remark 1.2: what the algebraic conjectures contain
items.statement: (i) All the groups are finite dimensional over the appropriate field (Q_p, K, F). (ii) The period isomorphism gives dim_{Q_p}H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p) = dim_K H^i_dR(X). (iii) H^i_HK(X) is an F-vector space with semilinear ϕ and monodromy N satisfying Nϕ = pϕN, and there is a Hyodo–Kato isomorphism ι_HK : H^i_HK(X) ⊗_F K ≅ H^i_dR(X). (iv) In C_dR the filtration on the left comes from B_dR and on the right is the tensor product of the Hodge filtration with that of B_dR; in C_st the ϕ and N on the left come from B_st and on the right are the tensor products. (v) Galois descent recovers de Rham and Hyodo–Kato cohomology: H^i_dR(X) ≅ (H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p) ⊗ B_dR)^{G_K} as filtered K-vector spaces and H^i_HK(X) ≅ (H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p) ⊗ B_st)^{G_K} as F-vector spaces with ϕ and N, the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism being induced by B_st ⊂ B_dR; equivalently H^i_dR(X)^* ≅ Hom_{G_K}(H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p),B_dR) and H^i_HK(X)^* ≅ Hom_{G_K}(H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p),B_st). (vi) Q_p can be extracted from B_st, which gives a de Rham-to-étale bicartesian diagram with corners H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p), (H^i_HK(X) ⊗_F B_st)^{N=0,ϕ=1}, F^0(H^i_dR(X) ⊗_K B_dR) and H^i_dR(X) ⊗_K B_dR; twisting by r ≥ i removes the denominators in t and gives the same diagram with Q_p(r), (H^i_HK ⊗_F B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r}, F^r(H^i_dR ⊗_K B^+_dR) and H^i_dR ⊗_K B^+_dR. (vii) The pair (H^i_HK(X),H^i_dR(X)) is a filtered (ϕ,N)-module in Fontaine's sense, and bicartesianness together with finite dimensionality of H^i_ét forces it to be weakly admissible.
items.note: This remark is the template the whole paper follows: each of its seven parts has an analytic counterpart among the conjectures and theorems below.

items.name: Remark 1.3: the status of the algebraic conjectures
items.statement: Fontaine's conjecture is a theorem, by four lines of attack — the almost étale approach, the syntomic approach, the motivic approach and the derived geometry approach — whose period isomorphisms have been compared; the most comprehensive results are Beilinson's, with no assumption of properness, good models or smoothness. Without a semistable model over O_K, H^i_HK(X) must be replaced by H^i_HK(X_K̄), which is an F^nr-vector space with a semilinear G_K-action commuting with ϕ and N, the action being smooth (every element is fixed by G_L for some finite L/K depending on it); the descent statements then involve smooth vectors, H^i_HK(X_K̄)^* ≅ Hom^sm_{G_K}(H^i_ét(X_C,Q_p),B_st) as (ϕ,N,G_K)-modules over F^nr.

items.name: The class of varieties: smooth dagger varieties
items.statement: The paper works with smooth dagger varieties over K or C, with no assumption on the existence of good models. Any proper or partially proper rigid analytic variety has a natural dagger structure, which covers analytifications of algebraic varieties, Stein varieties (for example étale coverings of Drinfeld's spaces in any dimension) and, more generally, holomorphically convex varieties (proper fibrations over a Stein base); dagger varieties that are not partially proper include overconvergent affinoids and, more generally, quasi-compact rigid analytic varieties with an overconvergent structure. Étale cohomology is replaced throughout by pro-étale cohomology, so the theory is rational rather than integral p-adic Hodge theory: the pro-étale cohomology of the analytification of an algebraic variety is much bigger than the étale cohomology of that variety, which is finite dimensional.

items.name: Conjecture 1.4: the de Rham-to-pro-étale C_dR + C_st
items.statement: Let X be a smooth dagger variety over C and let i ≤ r. Then there is a functorial bicartesian diagram with corners H^i_proét(X,Q_p(r)), (H^i_HK(X) ⊗̂_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r}, H^i(F^rRΓ_dR(X/B^+_dR)) and H^i_dR(X/B^+_dR).
items.note: The analytic analogue of Remark 1.2(vi). Proved here for small varieties with de Rham slopes ≥ 0 (Theorem 1.11), and for dagger affinoids directly (Theorem 6.14).

items.name: Remark 1.5: what the diagram of Conjecture 1.4 means
items.statement: (i) H^i_dR(X/B^+_dR) is a torsion-free B^+_dR-module from which usual de Rham cohomology is recovered modulo t, and for X over K one has H^i_dR(X_C/B^+_dR) ≅ H^i_dR(X) ⊗̂_K B^+_dR. (ii) For X over K all spaces carry a natural topology and a G_K-action and all maps are G_K-equivariant and continuous. (iii) For X over C all spaces have a natural topology and, by the authors' earlier work, a VS structure. (v) For proper analytic varieties all the groups in the diagram are finite dimensional and the kernels of the horizontal arrows are 0; for a general analytic variety this fails and the spaces must be seen in the derived category of locally convex topological Q_p-vector spaces, the tensor products being derived completed tensor products — even when H^i_dR(X) is finite dimensional, H^i(F^r(B^+_dR ⊗̂_K RΓ_dR(X))) surjects onto Ω^i(X_C)^{d=0} and so can be huge, and then so is H^i_proét(X_C,Q_p(r)).

items.name: Conjecture 1.6: the pro-étale-to-de Rham conjectures over K
items.statement: For X a smooth dagger variety over K there are functorial isomorphisms: (C_dR) H^i_dR(X)^* ≅ Hom_{G_K}(H^i_proét(X_C,Q_p),B_dR) as filtered K-vector spaces; (C_st) H^i_HK(X)^* ≅ Hom^sm_{G_K}(H^i_proét(X_C,Q_p),B_st) as (ϕ,N,G_K)-modules over F^nr.
items.note: Remark 1.7 observes that it is "a little bit of a miracle" that the finite dimensional H^i_dR(X) can be recovered from the huge H^i_proét(X_C,Q_p).

items.name: Conjecture 1.8: the pro-étale-to-de Rham conjectures over C
items.statement: For X a smooth dagger variety over C there are functorial isomorphisms: (C_dR) Hom_{B^+_dR}(H^i_dR(X/B^+_dR),B_dR) ≅ Hom_VS(H^i_proét(X,Q_p),B_dR) as B_dR-modules; (C_st) Hom_{F^nr}(H^i_HK(X),B_st) ≅ Hom_VS(H^i_proét(X,Q_p),B_st) as B_st-modules. Over C there is no Galois action, so the VS structure replaces it.

items.name: Remark 1.9: what the VS structure cannot see
items.statement: (i) The filtration on B^+_dR-cohomology cannot be recovered at the level of cohomology because the t^kB^+_dR are all isomorphic as VS's while they are pairwise distinct as G_K-modules. (ii) Likewise ϕ and N disappear, since M = M^{N=0,ϕ=1} ⊗_{B^{ϕ=1}_cris} B_st when M = M_0 ⊗_{F^nr} B_st for a finite rank (ϕ,N)-module M_0 over F^nr. (iii) One way to read this: Conjecture 1.4 represents H^i_proét as the H^0 of a quasi-coherent sheaf on the Fargues–Fontaine curve obtained as the modification at ∞ of the sheaf attached to a ϕ-module; the H^0 determines the sheaf, because there is no H^1, but not the modification that produced it, and a formulation at the level of derived categories might.
items.note: A structural limitation, not a gap in a proof: it is why Conjectures 1.6 and 1.8 have different shapes.

items.name: Small varieties and de Rham slopes ≥ 0
items.statement: A smooth dagger variety is small if its de Rham cohomology is finite dimensional. A small variety has de Rham slopes ≥ 0 if, for every i, the slopes of the vector bundle on the Fargues–Fontaine curve associated with the filtered (ϕ,N)-module (H^i_HK(X), F^0H^i(X/B_dR)) are ≥ 0 — which holds in particular when those filtered (ϕ,N)-modules are weakly admissible, the associated bundles then having all slopes 0.
items.note: These two conditions are the hypotheses of the main theorem; the second is conjectured to be automatic (Remark 1.10(ii)).

items.name: Remark 1.10: which varieties are small, and with which slopes
items.statement: (i) Small varieties include proper varieties, overconvergent affinoids, quasi-compact dagger varieties, analytifications of algebraic varieties, and certain tubular neighbourhoods of subvarieties of proper varieties or the complements of such. (ii) The authors conjecture that every small variety has de Rham slopes ≥ 0; the cases known are proper varieties, overconvergent affinoids, analytifications of algebraic varieties and various complements of tubular neighbourhoods, and a product of two small varieties with de Rham slopes ≥ 0 is again one. (iii) It is conceivable that all complements of tubular neighbourhoods of subvarieties of proper varieties have de Rham slopes ≥ 0, and — optimistically — that any quasi-compact dagger variety is such a complement.
items.note: The conjecture in (ii) and the speculations in (iii) are recorded as gaps: a design job must not plan them as results.

items.name: Theorem 1.11: the main theorem
items.statement: If X is small and has de Rham slopes ≥ 0 then Conjecture 1.4 holds; and if X is defined over K then Conjecture 1.6 holds, while if X is defined over C then Conjecture 1.8 holds.

items.name: Theorem 1.12: the height of pro-étale cohomology
items.statement: If X is small with de Rham slopes ≥ 0 then ht(H^i_proét(X_C,Q_p)) = dim_C(H^i_dR(X_C)). The VS's in the diagram of Conjecture 1.4 are extensions of finite Dimensional Vector Spaces — Banach–Colmez spaces, written BC — by torsion B^+_dR-Modules; such objects, called qBC's, carry a height ht(W) ∈ Z, normalised so that the qBC attached to a finite dimensional Q_p-vector space W has ht = dim_{Q_p}W.
items.note: The analytic analogue of Remark 1.2(ii), and surprising because the pro-étale cohomology it constrains is in general infinite dimensional.

items.name: Remark 1.13: which theory of BC's each case needs
items.statement: The proof of Theorem 1.11 makes heavy use of the theory of Banach–Colmez spaces, in particular of the geometric point of view of Le Bras's thesis, and about half the paper is devoted to results about BC's that the main theorem needs. For proper varieties the naive theory of BC's used in the authors' earlier paper suffices; for an overconvergent affinoid or a small Stein variety there is a direct proof from the basic comparison theorem of part I.

items.name: Remark 1.14: the Stein case
items.statement: If X is smooth and Stein over C or K it is a strict increasing union of overconvergent affinoids, and then the horizontal rows of the diagram of Conjecture 1.4 are surjective with kernels (Ω^{i−1}(X)/ker d)(r−i); in particular there is an exact sequence 0 → Ω^{r−1}(X)/ker d → H^r_proét(X,Q_p(r)) → (H^r_HK(X) ⊗̂_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r} → 0, which generalises the exact sequence of Colmez–Dospinescu–Nizioł's Theorem 1.8, proved there under the assumption that X has a semistable model. Conjectures 1.4, 1.6 and 1.8 are not difficult to deduce in this case.
items.note: This is exactly the sequence PAPER-COLMEZ-DOSPINESCU-NIZIOL-20 proves for semistable Stein weak formal schemes; here the semistability hypothesis is removed.

items.name: The inputs from part I: the basic comparison isomorphism and the syntomic sequence
items.statement: For X a quasi-compact smooth dagger variety over C, part I supplies the basic comparison isomorphism H^i_syn(X,Q_p(r)) ≅ H^i_proét(X,Q_p(r)) for i ≤ r (1.15) and the long exact sequence ⋯ → DR^{i−1}_r(X) → H^i_syn(X,Q_p(r)) → HK^i_r(X) --ι_HK--> DR^i_r(X) → ⋯ (1.16), where HK^i_r(X) := (H^i_HK(X) ⊗̂_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r} and DR^i_r(X) := H^i(RΓ_dR(X/B^+_dR)/F^r). Both the isomorphism and the sequence can be promoted to the category of VS's, which is what the rest of the paper needs.
items.note: Quoted from the authors' part I, 'On the cohomology of p-adic analytic spaces, I: The basic comparison theorem' (J. Algebraic Geom. 34 (2025), 1–108); that paper has no extraction in the atlas.

items.name: Proposition 1.17 (= Proposition 7.10): four equivalent conditions
items.statement: The following are equivalent: (a) the diagram of Conjecture 1.4 is bicartesian; (b) the slopes of the vector bundle associated with (H^i_HK(X), F^0H^i_dR(X/B_dR)) are ≥ 0 for i = r−1 and i = r; (c) the kernel and cokernel of H^r_proét(X,Q_p(r)) → (H^r_HK(X) ⊗_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r} have height 0; (d) ht(H^r_proét(X,Q_p(r))) = dim_C H^r_dR(X).
items.note: The key consequence of the theory of BC's: it converts the comparison theorem into a slope condition and a height computation. Its ingredients are the categorification of the height (Proposition 3.27), a statement about (ϕ,N)-modules (Lemma 5.17) and one about BC's (Proposition 3.23); the hypothesis that the degrees are ≤ r enters through Lemma 5.17, because it makes the slopes of Frobenius on Hyodo–Kato cohomology ≤ r.

items.name: The Hom-vanishing inputs for Conjectures 1.6 and 1.8
items.statement: Conjectures 1.6 and 1.8 follow from Conjecture 1.4 together with: Hom_{G_K}(B^+_dR/t^k,B_dR) = 0 (Proposition 2.14) and Hom_VS(B^+_dR/t^k,B_dR) = 0 (Corollary 3.18), which remove the de Rham terms from the sequence of Hom's deduced from the bicartesian diagram; and, for M a (ϕ,N)-module of slopes ≤ r, Hom_{G_K}((M ⊗_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r},B_dR) = M^*_K (Theorem 5.8 and its corollaries) and Hom_VS((M ⊗_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r},B_dR) = M^* ⊗_{F^nr} B_dR (Propositions 5.18 and 5.20).

items.name: Banach representations and the exact category B(G_K)
items.statement: A banach is a Banach space over Q_p up to equivalence of norms, and a banach representation of G_K is a banach with a continuous linear action of G_K; B(G_K) is their category. A short exact sequence in B(G_K) is 0 → B_1 → B_2 → B_3 → 0 with the second map a strict epimorphism and the first its kernel — by the open mapping theorem, equivalently both maps continuous and the sequence algebraically exact. A Q_p-representation of G_K is a finite dimensional Q_p-vector space with a continuous linear action, a C-representation a finite dimensional C-vector space with a continuous semilinear action, and more generally Rep_{B^+_dR}(G_K) is the category of finite length B^+_dR-representations. Throughout, k is perfect and countable, so that O_C/p ≅ O_{K̄}/p is countable.

items.name: Theorem 2.1: Fontaine — the forgetful functors are fully faithful
items.statement: If [K:Q_p] < ∞ the forgetful functors Rep_C(G_K) → B(G_K) and Rep_{B^+_dR}(G_K) → B(G_K) are fully faithful: every Q_p-linear continuous G_K-equivariant map between C-representations is automatically C-linear, and likewise B^+_dR-linear between B^+_dR-representations.
items.note: Quoted from Fontaine's 'Presque C_p-représentations'; it is what gives the notation Hom_{G_K} its meaning in §2.3.

items.name: Remark 2.2: the Sen-theoretic strengthening, and Hom(C,C) = K for any K
items.statement: The proof uses Sen's theory and gives more: the same statements hold for E-linear maps between E-representations whose Hodge–Tate–Sen weights are algebraic over E, a condition automatic for E = Q_p when [K:Q_p] < ∞. In particular the fundamental identity Hom_{G_K}(C,C) ≅ K is valid for arbitrary K, where Hom_{G_K} abbreviates Hom_{B(G_K)}, i.e. continuous G_K-equivariant Q_p-linear maps.

items.name: Almost C-representations and the category C(G_K)
items.statement: Two banach representations W_1, W_2 are almost isomorphic if there are finite dimensional G_K-stable Q_p-subspaces V_i ⊂ W_i with W_1/V_1 ≅ W_2/V_2. An almost C-representation is a banach representation almost isomorphic to C^d for some d, and C(G_K) is their category. The definition makes sense for arbitrary K, but the theory has a satisfactory shape only for [K:Q_p] < ∞, where C(G_K) is an abelian subcategory of the exact category B(G_K); the authors ask whether Fontaine's later point of view would give a satisfactory theory in general, and provide alternative proofs of the §2.3 results that they actually use, valid for arbitrary K. Modulo almost isomorphisms the category is semi-simple with a single isomorphism class of simple objects, that of C.

items.name: Dimension and height of an almost C-representation
items.statement: For W ∈ C(G_K) with [K:Q_p] < ∞ and W/V_2 ≅ C^d/V_1, one sets dim(W) = d and ht(W) = dim_{Q_p}(V_2) − dim_{Q_p}(V_1); this is independent of the choices and yields additive functions — a nontrivial fact whose proof uses the theory of Banach–Colmez spaces, namely that an effective BC of dimension 1 and height h mapping to C with non-finite-dimensional image maps onto it with kernel of dimension 0 and height h. One has dim(C) = 1, ht(C) = 0, and dim(V) = 0, ht(V) = dim_{Q_p}(V) for a Q_p-representation. Every B^+_dR-representation of length d lies in C(G_K), is almost isomorphic to C^d, and has dim = d, ht = 0; in particular C and C(1) are almost isomorphic.
items.note: Quoted from Fontaine. This ht is the Galois-side analogue of the height of a BC, and of the height of a qBC used in Theorem 1.12.

items.name: Proposition 2.5: Ext in C(G_K) is computed in Rep_{Q_p} and Rep_{B^+_dR}
items.statement: (i) For X, Y ∈ Rep_{Q_p}(G_K) the natural map Ext^i_{G_K}(X,Y) → Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(X,Y) is an isomorphism for all i ≥ 0. (ii) For X, Y ∈ Rep_{B^+_dR}(G_K) the natural map Ext^i_{B^+_dR(G_K)}(X,Y) → Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(X,Y) is an isomorphism for all i ≥ 0. This is the device by which Fontaine reduced the computation of Ext-groups in C(G_K) to their computation in the two smaller categories. Hypothesis: [K:Q_p] < ∞.
items.note: Quoted from Fontaine. Used in the proof of Proposition 2.7 and in Remark 3.22 to transfer a BC argument to almost C-representations.

items.name: Theorem 2.6: finiteness, Euler characteristic and duality in C(G_K)
items.statement: For X, Y ∈ C(G_K) with [K:Q_p] < ∞: (i) the Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(X,Y) are finite rank Q_p-vector spaces, trivial for i ≥ 3; (ii) Σ_{i=0}^2 (−1)^i dim_{Q_p}Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(X,Y) = −[K:Q_p]·ht(X)·ht(Y); (iii) there is a natural trace map Ext^2_{C(G_K)}(X,X(1)) → Q_p and for 0 ≤ i ≤ 2 the pairing Ext^i(X,Y) × Ext^{2−i}(Y,X(1)) → Ext^2(X,X(1)) → Q_p is a perfect duality.
items.note: Quoted from Fontaine. Used in Lemma 2.10 and Example 2.12.

items.name: The cyclotomic data and the twisted uniformizer t′
items.statement: Let χ be the cyclotomic character, K_∞ ⊂ K(µ_{p^∞}) the cyclotomic Z_p-extension, γ a topological generator of Gal(K_∞/K), and {ζ_{p^n}} a compatible system of primitive p^n-th roots of unity with t ∈ B^+_dR the associated uniformizer. One also uses Fontaine's twisted form t′ := t/π_t, a uniformizer of B^+_dR fixed by Gal(K̄/K_∞), whereas t is only fixed by Gal(K̄/K(µ_{p^∞})).
items.note: It is t′ that makes the complex of Proposition 2.7 Gal(K_∞/K)-equivariant.

items.name: Proposition 2.7: the complex computing Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(C,W)
items.statement: For W a B^+_dR-representation the groups Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(C,W) are computed by the three-term complex W(0) --x↦(t′x,(γ−1)x)--> W(1) ⊕ W(0) --(x,y)↦t′y−(χ^{−1}(γ)γ−1)x--> W(1), where W(0) is the space of generalized invariants — the elements killed by (g_1−1)⋯(g_r−1) for all g_i ∈ G_K and r large — and W(1) = t′((t′)^{−1}W)^{(0)}. The proof observes that Proposition 2.5 makes Ext^i_{B^+_dR(G_K)}(C,W) → Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(C,W) an isomorphism (2.8), and then quotes Fontaine's computation.
items.note: The engine for Corollary 2.9, Lemma 2.10 and Example 2.12.

items.name: Corollary 2.9: vanishing between truncations of B^+_dR in the range i < j
items.statement: For N ≥ 0 and 1 ≤ i < j, Hom_{C(G_K)}(B^+_dR/t^i, t^{−N}B^+_dR/t^j) = 0 and Ext^1_{C(G_K)}(B^+_dR/t^i, t^{−N}B^+_dR/t^j) = 0. By dévissage and twisting one reduces to i = 1, where W = t^{−N}B^+_dR/t^j has W(0) = K and W(1) = Kt′, multiplication by t′ is an isomorphism between them and the other maps vanish, so the complex of Proposition 2.7 is acyclic.
items.note: The proof in fact shows the whole complex is acyclic, so Ext^2 vanishes as well. The printed twisting index reuses the letter j already bound in the statement, where the graded pieces are C(m) for 0 ≤ m ≤ i−1.

items.name: Lemma 2.10: all Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(B^+_dR/t^k, C(j))
items.statement: For j ∈ Z and k ≥ 1: Ext^0 is K if j = 0 and 0 otherwise; Ext^1 is K if j = 0 or j = k and 0 otherwise; Ext^2 is K if j = k and 0 otherwise. The proof applies Proposition 2.7 to W = (B^+_dR/t^k)(1−j) together with the duality of Theorem 2.6 between Ext^i(C,W) and Ext^{2−i}(W,C(1)); one computes W(0) = Kt^{j−1}(1−j) for 1 ≤ j ≤ k and 0 otherwise, W(1) ≅ Kt′t^{j−1}(1−j) for 0 ≤ j ≤ k−1 and 0 otherwise, and in the complex the only nonzero maps are the multiplications by t′, isomorphisms except when exactly one of the two groups vanishes, i.e. when j = 0 or j = k.
items.note: The answers are consistent with the Euler characteristic of Theorem 2.6(ii), which vanishes here since both heights are 0. The printed range for W(1) reads "0 ≤ j ≤ j−1", an empty condition; the following clause fixes it as 0 ≤ j ≤ k−1.

items.name: Remark 2.11: the non-trivial extensions of B^+_dR/t^k by C(k)
items.statement: Every non-trivial extension of B^+_dR/t^k by C(k) is isomorphic to B^+_dR/t^{k+1}.
items.note: Immediate from Ext^1(B^+_dR/t^k,C(k)) ≅ K being a line.

items.name: Example 2.12: extensions of Tate twists
items.statement: Ext^1_{C(G_K)}(C,C) ≅ K, generated by the class of C ⊗ (Q_p ⊕ Q_p log t); since Ext^0(C,C) ≅ K by Remark 2.2, Theorem 2.6 forces Ext^2_{C(G_K)}(C,C) = 0. By duality Ext^1_{C(G_K)}(C,C(1)) ≅ K, generated by the class of B^+_dR/t^2, and Ext^2_{C(G_K)}(C,C(1)) ≅ K; all the other Ext^i_{C(G_K)}(C,C(j)) vanish.

items.name: Proposition 2.13: the two inputs valid for arbitrary K
items.statement: (i) Hom_{G_K}(C,C) ≅ K. (ii) K̄ is dense in B^+_dR. Fontaine's proof of (i) works for arbitrary K, whereas the alternative proof by class field theory works only for [K:Q_p] < ∞; (ii) is Colmez's construction of B_dR.
items.note: §2.3 opens with "In this section, K is arbitrary"; these two facts are what the general-K proof of Proposition 2.14 rests on.

items.name: Vector Spaces over sympathetic algebras
items.statement: A Vector Space (VS) W is a functor Λ ↦ W(Λ) from sympathetic algebras to Q_p-vector spaces, and a sequence 0 → W_1 → W → W_2 → 0 is exact precisely when it is exact on W(Λ) for every Λ. Sympathetic algebras are, following Colmez, the spectral connected C-Banach algebras Λ on which x ↦ x^p is surjective on {x : ‖x−1‖_Λ < 1}, with O_Λ the unit ball; this paper imposes two further conditions, that Λ → C(Spm(Λ) → C) be injective — a property taken for granted in the earlier arguments but failing for instance for Λ = O_{C′} with C′ the spherical closure of C — and that Λ be separable, i.e. have a dense C-subspace of countable dimension, so that Hahn–Banach is available without assuming C spherically complete. Since O_C/p is countable, the sympathetic closure of a separable such algebra is again separable.
items.note: The two additional requirements are corrections introduced by this paper relative to the original definition.

items.name: The basic Vector Spaces: V_d, Fontaine rings, B_m and U_{h,d}
items.statement: Trivial examples of VS's are the finite dimensional Q_p-vector spaces V (constant functor) and V_d with V_d(Λ) = Λ^d. Fontaine's rings B^+_cris, B^+_st, B^+_dR, B_cris, B_st, B_dR are naturally VS's and even Rings; B_m := B^+_dR/t^mB^+_dR is a VS and a Ring for m ≥ 1; and for h ≥ 1, d ∈ Z one has U_{h,d} = (B^+_cris)^{ϕ^h=p^d} if d ≥ 0 and U_{h,d} = B_{−d}/Q_p^h if d < 0.
items.note: V_1 (the VS Λ ↦ Λ, with V_1(C) = C) is the reference object for curvature; B_m and U_{h,d} are the building blocks of every BC.

items.name: BC (finite Dimensional Vector Space) and its Dimension
items.statement: Morally a BC is a finite dimensional C-vector space up to a finite dimensional Q_p-vector space, with Dimension Dim W = (a,b) where a = dim W is the C-dimension and b = ht W ∈ Z the Q_p-dimension. Precisely, a VS W is finite Dimensional — a BC — if it equals V_d up to finite dimensional Q_p-vector spaces: there are finite dimensional Q_p-vector spaces V_1, V_2 and exact sequences 0 → V_1 → Y → V_d → 0 and 0 → V_2 → Y → W → 0, so that W is obtained from V_d by adding V_1 and quotienting by V_2; then dim W = d and ht W = dim_{Q_p}V_1 − dim_{Q_p}V_2. These are the objects often called Banach–Colmez spaces.
items.note: The order of the two dimensions is opposite to §2.2.1 because the two presentations are opposite; both give ht(V) = dim V for a Q_p-space and ht(C) = 0. The auxiliary letters V_1, V_2 here are finite dimensional Q_p-spaces, not the VS V_1 of §3.1.1.

items.name: Remark 3.1: why the functor, and the faithfulness of C-points
items.statement: (i) One is in general only interested in W = W(C), but without the extra structure its Dimension could not be spoken of — for example C and C ⊕ Q_p are isomorphic as topological Q_p-vector spaces. (ii) The functor W ↦ W(C) is faithful on BC's; moreover W(Λ) is a Q_p-banach for every Λ, a morphism of BC's induces continuous strict maps W_1(Λ) → W_2(Λ), and an exact sequence of BC's induces a strictly exact sequence for every sympathetic Λ.
items.note: This is what licenses passing freely between a BC and its C-points, as the paper does whenever it writes ht(H^i_proét).

items.name: Proposition 3.2: Dimension is well defined and additive; BC is abelian
items.statement: (i) The Dimension of a BC is independent of the choices in its definition. (ii) For f : W_1 → W_2 a morphism of BC's, ker f, coker f and im f are BC's, with Dim W_1 = Dim ker f + Dim im f and Dim W_2 = Dim coker f + Dim im f. (iii) If dim W = 0 then ht W ≥ 0. (iv) If W has an increasing filtration with successive quotients V_1, then every sub-BC W′ has ht W′ ≥ 0. The category BC of BC's is abelian.
items.note: Quoted from the authors' earlier paper, itself resting on Colmez. (ii) is the additivity behind every Dimension count in §3.

items.name: The Dimensions of B_m and U_{h,d}
items.statement: The Spaces B_m and U_{h,d} are BC's, with Dim B_m = (m,0) and Dim U_{h,d} = (d,h) if d ≥ 0, (−d,−h) if d < 0.

items.name: Curvature of a BC
items.statement: For W ∈ BC one says W has curvature > 0 if Hom(W,V_1) = 0; curvature ≥ 0 if Hom(W,B^+_dR) = 0; curvature = 0, or affine, if it is a successive extension of V_1's; curvature < 0 if it injects into B_dR^d, equivalently into (B^+_dR)^d; curvature ≤ 0 if it injects into a B^+_dR-Module, i.e. a VS with an action of B^+_dR.
items.note: Curvature > 0 implies curvature ≥ 0, by dévissage from 0 → V_1 → B_m → B_{m−1} → 0 and B^+_dR = lim_k B_k.

items.name: Remark 3.6: elementary properties of curvature
items.statement: (i) If W has curvature > 0 (resp. ≥ 0) and W′ has curvature ≤ 0 (resp. < 0), then Hom_BC(W,W′) = 0. (ii) A sub-VS of one of curvature ≤ 0 (resp. < 0) has curvature ≤ 0 (resp. < 0). (iii) A quotient of one of curvature ≥ 0 (resp. > 0) has curvature ≥ 0 (resp. > 0).

items.name: Proposition 3.7: the canonical filtration of a BC
items.statement: Every W ∈ BC has a unique filtration W_{>0} ⊂ W_{≥0} ⊂ W, the canonical filtration, with W_{>0} of curvature > 0, W_{≥0}/W_{>0} of curvature 0 and W/W_{≥0} of curvature < 0. One defines W_{>0} as the intersection of the kernels of all morphisms W → B_m, m ≥ 1, and W_{≥0} as the intersection of the kernels of all morphisms W → B_dR; the outer two properties are then clear, while the curvature-0 property of the middle piece comes from the description of the canonical filtration in terms of the Harder–Narasimhan filtration in §3.2.8. One writes W_{≤0} := W/W_{>0}, the largest quotient of curvature ≤ 0, and W_{=0} := W_{≥0}/W_{>0}, the largest affine sub-VS of W_{≤0}. The filtration and a number of results about it are due to Plût; most of them can be recovered from the relation of BC to vector bundles on the Fargues–Fontaine curve and Le Bras's Harder–Narasimhan theory.
items.note: The symbols W_{>0}, W_{≥0} are also used in §3.2.5 for the Harder–Narasimhan filtration at λ = 0, and the two differ; §3.2.8 spells out the relation.

items.name: The algebraic Fargues–Fontaine curve
items.statement: The Fargues–Fontaine curve X = X_FF is the projective scheme attached to the graded Q_p-algebra ⊕_{d≥0}U_d with U_d = (B^+_cris)^{ϕ=p^d}. Its closed points correspond to the Q_p-lines of U_1, and for x ∈ X one fixes a basis t_x of the corresponding line; C corresponds to a specific point ∞ with t = t_∞ Fontaine's p-adic 2πi. The residue field C_x is algebraically closed and complete for v_p with C_x^♭ = C^♭, but need not be isomorphic to C; the residue field at ∞ is C itself, and the completed local ring at x is B^+_dR(C_x) with uniformizer t_x, equal to B^+_dR when x = ∞.
items.note: The distinction between ∞ and the other points is exactly what separates curvature 0 from curvature > 0.

items.name: Harder–Narasimhan categories, and Coh_X as one
items.statement: A Harder–Narasimhan category is an exact category with additive real valued rank and degree functions satisfying extra conditions, giving a slope µ = deg/rk with values in R ∐ {±∞}. An object E is of slope λ if µ(E) = λ, semistable if µ(E′) ≤ µ(E) for every strict subobject, stable if the inequality is strict. Every object carries a canonical decreasing filtration by strict subobjects E_{≥λ}, with E_{≥λ}/E_{>λ} semistable of slope λ where E_{>λ} = ∪_{µ>λ}E_{≥µ}; E has slopes ≥ λ (resp. > λ) if E = E_{≥λ} (resp. E_{>λ}) and slopes ≤ λ (resp. < λ) if E_{>λ} = 0 (resp. E_{≥λ} = 0). Consequently Hom(E_1,E_2) = 0 if E_1 has slopes ≥ λ and E_2 slopes < λ, a quotient of an object of slopes ≥ λ has slopes ≥ λ, and a subobject of one of slopes ≤ λ has slopes ≤ λ. For a vector bundle on X one has rk, deg and µ = deg/rk, extended to torsion coherent sheaves by additivity, so that torsion sheaves have rank 0, degree > 0 and slope +∞; endowed with rk and deg, the category Coh_X of coherent sheaves on X is a Harder–Narasimhan category.
items.note: The fourth consequence listed in the paper, that an extension of an object of slopes ≤ λ_2 by one of slopes ≥ λ_1 has slopes in [λ_1,λ_2], is false as printed: O(5) ⊕ O has slopes ≥ 0 and ≤ 1 in its two factors but a slope 5. Two-sided hypotheses on both terms are needed.

items.name: Theorem 3.9: the Fargues–Fontaine classification
items.statement: (i) For λ = d/h in lowest terms there is, up to isomorphism, a unique stable vector bundle O(λ) of slope λ, of rank h and degree d. (ii) Every vector bundle on X is a direct sum O(λ_1) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ O(λ_r); in particular the Harder–Narasimhan filtration splits non-canonically. (iii) Every coherent sheaf is a direct sum O(λ_1) ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ O(λ_r) ⊕ (⊕_{x∈X}F_x) with F_x torsion supported at x and zero for almost all x, the λ_i being the slopes, to which +∞ must be added when some F_x is nonzero.
items.note: Quoted from Fargues–Fontaine. Used with (3.10) to characterise acyclic (ϕ,N)-modules.

items.name: The cohomology of O(λ) and its Dimension
items.statement: For λ = d/h in lowest terms: H^0(X,O(λ)) = (B^+_cris)^{ϕ^h=p^d} and H^1(X,O(λ)) = 0 if λ ≥ 0; H^0(X,O(λ)) = 0 and H^1(X,O(λ)) = B^+_dR/(t^{−d}B^+_dR ⊕ Q_p^h) if λ < 0. Each H^i is the space of C-points of a BC, with Dim H^0 = (d,h) and Dim H^1 = 0 for λ ≥ 0, Dim H^0 = 0 and Dim H^1 = (−d,−h) for λ < 0. For λ ≥ 0 the groups clearly depend only on C^♭; for λ < 0 this is less clear, since t depends on C, but remains true.
items.note: Quoted from Fargues–Fontaine; this identifies the H^0/H^1 of line bundles with the U_{h,d}.

items.name: Remark 3.11: the Euler–Poincaré formula for heights
items.statement: From the formulas (3.10), ht(H^0(X,O(λ))) − ht(H^1(X,O(λ))) = h for every λ; by additivity this gives ht(H^0(X,E)) − ht(H^1(X,E)) = rk E for every vector bundle E on X, and the formula extends to coherent sheaves.
items.note: This is the mechanism turning height statements into rank statements, used in Proposition 7.10 and Corollary 7.9.

items.name: Coh^-_X and Le Bras’s functor BC
items.statement: Le Bras shows that the sheaf W^sh on Perf_C associated to a BC satisfies W^sh(Λ) = W(Λ) for every sympathetic Λ, and that W ↦ W^sh identifies BC with the smallest sub-abelian category of pro-étale sheaves on Perf_C stable under extensions and containing Q_p and V_1 — an efficient alternative definition. Coh^-_X is the subcategory of D^b(Coh_X) of complexes with cohomology only in degrees −1 and 0, with H^{−1} of slopes < 0 and H^0 of slopes ≥ 0; every object is represented by a zero map E_{−1} → E_0 with H^0(X,E_{−1}) = 0 and H^1(X,E_0) = 0. Le Bras defines an exact functor BC : Coh^-_X → BC, sending a complex F to the sheaf associated to the presheaf of degree-0 hypercohomology of X_S with values in F_S, and by construction there is an exact sequence 0 → H^1(X,E_{−1}) → BC(E_{−1} → E_0) → H^0(X,E_0) → 0; more generally BC(E^•) is an extension of H^0(X,H^0(E^•)) by H^1(X,H^{−1}(E^•)). Morphisms are computed by the upper-triangular matrix with entries Hom(E_{−1},F_{−1}), Ext^1(E_0,F_{−1}) and Hom(E_0,F_0).
items.note: The Hom-matrix is the computational tool for all the Hom and Ext computations of §§3.2.6–3.2.7 and of Lemma 3.16.

items.name: Theorem 3.12: Le Bras — Coh^-_X ≃ BC
items.statement: The functor BC realises an equivalence of categories Coh^-_X ≃ BC.
items.note: Quoted from Le Bras, whose main result it is. Everything from §3.2.5 to Proposition 3.23 is proved through it; §1.3.1 announces it as 'the more powerful point of view advocated in Le Bras' thesis'.

items.name: The Harder–Narasimhan structure on BC and the objects U_λ
items.statement: One endows Coh^-_X with rk^-(E_{−1} → E_0) = deg(E_0) − deg(E_{−1}) and deg^-(E_{−1} → E_0) = rk(E_{−1}) − rk(E_0), making it a Harder–Narasimhan category, and transports this to BC, where rk^- = dim and deg^- = −ht; a torsion F_x gives µ^-(BC(0 → F_x)) = 0. One writes W_{≥λ}, W_{>λ} for the Harder–Narasimhan filtration and W_{>−∞} := ∪_λ W_{≥λ}. For λ = d/h in lowest terms, U_λ := U_{h,d}, with U_{eh,ed} = U_λ^e for e ≥ 1, and U_λ = H^0(X,O(λ)) = BC(0 → O(λ)) if λ ≥ 0, U_λ = H^1(X,O(λ)) = BC(O(λ) → 0) if λ < 0; then rk^-(U_λ) = sign(λ)d, deg^-(U_λ) = −sign(λ)h and µ^-(U_λ) = −1/λ.
items.note: The slope on BC is the negative reciprocal of the curve slope; this sign-and-inversion convention governs every "slopes ≥ 0" statement of the paper.

items.name: Remark 3.13: BC’s as diamonds, and the decomposition (3.14)
items.statement: (i) Since Q_p = U_0, µ^-(Q_p) = −∞. (ii) BC's are naturally diamonds — among the first non-trivial examples — and as such have connected components: W_{>−∞} is the connected component of 0 and the quotient W_{−∞} is the largest étale quotient, a finite dimensional Q_p-vector space. (iii) The Harder–Narasimhan filtration splits non-canonically and every BC decomposes as (3.14) W = U_{−1/λ_1} ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ U_{−1/λ_r} ⊕ (⊕_x H^0(X,F_x)), with λ_i nonzero in Q ∪ {−∞}, U_{−1/λ_i} of slope λ_i, and F_x torsion supported at x and zero for almost all x with H^0(X,F_x) of slope 0; the λ_i are the slopes of W, to which 0 is added if some F_x is nonzero. (iv) In the sequence of §3.2.4, H^1(X,E_{−1}) is the subspace of slopes > 0 of BC(E_{−1} → E_0).
items.note: (3.14) is the structural workhorse, quoted in Corollary 3.18, §3.2.8, Lemma 3.24 and Remark 4.2.

items.name: Remark 3.15: a decreasing sequence of BC’s is stationary
items.statement: (i) The exact sequence 0 → W_{>−∞} → W → W_{−∞} → 0 makes it possible to show that a decreasing sequence (W_n) of BC's is stationary: dim(W_n) is decreasing and bounded below, hence constant for n ≥ N; then W_N/W_n has dimension 0 and is a quotient of W_N^{−∞}, and ht(W_N/W_n) is increasing and bounded by ht(W_N^{−∞}) < ∞, so W_N/W_n and hence W_n are eventually constant. (ii) Alternatively one uses a presentation to reduce to W = V_d and induces on d, using that a sub-BC of V_1 is either V_1 or a finite dimensional Q_p-vector space; this proof applies verbatim to almost C-representations.
items.note: Needed for Proposition 3.7 and invoked again in Lemma 8.10 to kill the R^1lim of a tower of BC’s.

items.name: Lemma 3.16: a sub-BC of V_N containing no V_1 has dim < ht
items.statement: A sub-BC W of V_N containing no V_1 satisfies dim(W) < ht(W), equivalently has slopes < −1. Through the equivalence Coh^-_X ≃ BC one decomposes W into stable pieces and reduces to U_λ with λ = d/h > 0, so that the claim becomes: if f : U_λ → V_N is injective then h > d. In Coh^-_X the corresponding map O(λ) → ι_{∞,*}C^N factors through Ô_{X,∞} ⊗ O(λ) → (ι_{∞,*}C) ⊗ O(λ) ≅ ι_{∞,*}C^h, giving an injection U_λ → V_h; since Dim U_λ = (d,h) and Dim V_h = (h,0), the existence of an injection forces h > d.
items.note: The statement is quoted from Colmez but reproved here via the curve. The final inequality is printed "h < d", the reverse of what the proof sets out to show ("we need to show that ... h > d") and of the lemma itself; and the reduction omits the λ = 0 summand Q_p, which "contains no V_1" does not exclude, though the conclusion is trivial there.

items.name: Morphisms between the U_λ
items.statement: Hom and Ext^1 in BC can be described through the curve. If D_λ is the division algebra with centre Q_p and invariant λ then End_BC(U_λ) = End(O(λ)) = D_λ. For λ_1 = d_1/h_1, λ_2 = d_2/h_2 and λ_1+λ_2 = d/h in minimal form, O(λ_1) ⊗ O(λ_2) = O(λ_1+λ_2)^{n(λ_1,λ_2)} with n(λ_1,λ_2) = h_1h_2/h, while Hom(O(λ_1),O(λ_2)) = Hom(O,O(λ_2−λ_1)) and Hom(O,O(λ)) = H^0(X,O(λ)). If λ = d/h ≥ 0 then Hom(U_λ,V_1) is the C-module of rank h generated by the θ∘ϕ^i, 0 ≤ i ≤ h−1.
items.note: The last computation shows that U_λ with λ ≥ 0 is not of curvature > 0, matching §3.2.8.

items.name: Torsion sheaves at a point and the BC’s U_m/Q_p t_x^m
items.statement: For x a closed point, F ↦ H^0(X,F) is an equivalence from torsion coherent sheaves supported at x to finite length B^+_dR(C_x)-modules; such a module is a sum of B_m(C_x) = B^+_dR(C_x)/t_x^m, and the sequence 0 → O --t_x^m--> O(m) → i_{x,*}B_m → 0 together with H^1(X,O) = 0 gives H^0(X,i_{x,*}B_m) = U_m/Q_p t_x^m. Hence End_BC(U_m/Q_p t_x^m) ≅ B_m(C_x), so for m = 1 the endomorphisms are C_x; and for x ≠ ∞, Hom_BC(U_1/Q_p t_x, V_1) = 0 because the two sheaves are supported at distinct points. In the case x = ∞, crucial for the paper's results, t_x = t and U_m/Q_p t^m = B_m, and the object of BC attached to a finite length B^+_dR-module M is simply M ⊗_{B^+_dR} B^+_dR.
items.note: The objects at x ≠ ∞ have height 0 yet curvature > 0, the source of the asymmetry recorded in footnote 9. The printed Hom is written with index m on both sheaves although the left side is the m = 1 case.

items.name: Proposition 3.17: curvature-0 BC’s are the finite length B^+_dR-modules
items.statement: The functor M ↦ M ⊗_{B^+_dR} B^+_dR is an equivalence between the category of B^+_dR-modules of finite length and the subcategory of BC of objects of curvature 0.

items.name: Corollary 3.18: no VS-maps out of a torsion B^+_dR-Module
items.statement: (i) The kernel and cokernel of a morphism of objects of curvature 0 are of curvature 0. (ii) If W is a torsion B^+_dR-Module, i.e. annihilated by t^r for some r ≥ 1, then Hom_VS(W,B^+_dR) = 0 and Hom_VS(W,B_dR) = 0. For (ii) one writes W = W ⊗_{B^+_dR} B^+_dR by Proposition 3.17 and computes Hom_VS(W,B^+_dR) = lim_k Hom_{B^+_dR}(W,B^+_dR/t^k) = Hom_{B^+_dR}(W,B^+_dR) = 0; for B_dR one uses that a BC of dimension 1 is a quotient of Q_p^r ⊕ L_ℓ for L_ℓ the Graph of an additive element, hence one of dimension d a quotient of Q_p^r ⊕ L_{ℓ_1} ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ L_{ℓ_d}, so that the image of any α : W → B_dR factors through t^{−N}B^+_dR for some N.
items.note: This is the VS-analogue of Proposition 2.14(iv), announced in §1.3.2; it is what removes the de Rham terms from the Hom-sequences of §9. Universal covers of p-divisible groups can be used instead of Graphs.

items.name: The canonical filtration read off the Harder–Narasimhan decomposition
items.statement: For W a BC the relation between (3.14) and the filtration of Proposition 3.7 is: W_{>0} ≅ (⊕_{λ_i>0}U_{−1/λ_i}) ⊕ (⊕_{x≠∞}H^0(X,F_x)); W_{≤0} ≅ (⊕_{λ_i<0}U_{−1/λ_i}) ⊕ H^0(X,F_∞) = H^0(X, F_∞ ⊕ (⊕_{λ_i<0}O(−1/λ_i))); W_{<0} ≅ ⊕_{λ_i<0}U_{−1/λ_i}; W_{=0} ≅ H^0(X,F_∞). In particular W is of curvature < 0 if and only if its Harder–Narasimhan slopes are < 0, and if its slopes are > 0 then it is of curvature > 0.
items.note: This completes the proof of Proposition 3.7. The last clause is one-directional: curvature > 0 also allows the slope-0 pieces H^0(X,F_x) with x ≠ ∞.

items.name: Corollary 3.19: curvature ≤ 0 and < 0 in terms of sheaves
items.statement: (i) W is of curvature < 0 (resp. ≤ 0) if and only if W ≅ H^0(X,E) with E a vector bundle of slopes ≥ 0 (resp. the sum of such a bundle and a torsion sheaf supported at ∞). (ii) An extension of two BC's of curvature < 0 (resp. ≤ 0) is again of curvature < 0 (resp. ≤ 0).

items.name: Corollary 3.20: the sign of the curvature determines the sign of the height
items.statement: (a) Curvature 0 implies height 0; (b) curvature < 0 implies height > 0; (c) curvature > 0 implies height ≤ 0. For (c) one cannot replace height ≤ 0 by height < 0: for x ≠ ∞ the object U_1/Q_p t_x has height 0 but curvature > 0.
items.note: (b) needs W ≠ 0: the zero object has curvature < 0 and height 0. By Corollary 3.19(i) and Remark 3.11, curvature < 0 gives ht(W) = rk E, which is > 0 exactly when W ≠ 0. This corollary is the bridge from the slope conditions to the height statements of Theorem 1.12 and Proposition 1.17.

items.name: Corollary 3.21: curvature decreases on subobjects and increases on quotients
items.statement: (i) A sub-BC of one of curvature ≤ 0 (resp. < 0) has curvature ≤ 0 (resp. < 0). (ii) A sub-BC of height 0 of one of curvature ≤ 0 has curvature 0. (iii) A quotient of one of curvature ≥ 0 (resp. > 0) has curvature ≥ 0 (resp. > 0). (iv) A quotient of height 0 of one of curvature ≥ 0 has curvature 0.
items.note: (iv) is contradicted by the paper’s own footnote 9 on the same page: U_1/Q_p t_x with x ≠ ∞ is a height-0 quotient of itself, of curvature > 0, and is not of curvature 0 since its endomorphisms are C_x and it admits no nonzero map to V_1. The correct statement, by §3.2.8, is that such a quotient has Harder–Narasimhan slope 0, i.e. is ⊕_x H^0(X,F_x); curvature 0 follows only once the support is {∞}. The "≤ 0" side is not symmetric because curvature ≤ 0 already forces support at ∞. Nothing downstream uses (iv); only (ii) is invoked, in Remark 3.22.

items.name: Remark 3.22: a sub-BC of a torsion B^+_dR-Module
items.statement: A sub-BC U of a torsion B^+_dR-Module W satisfies ht(U) ≥ 0, and is itself a torsion B^+_dR-Module if and only if ht(U) = 0. This can also be proved without the Harder–Narasimhan decomposition, by induction on the length of W, using that a sub-BC of V_1 is either V_1 or a finite dimensional Q_p-vector space and that an extension of B^+_dR-Modules is one; that proof extends verbatim to almost C-representations, thanks to Proposition 2.5.

items.name: Proposition 3.23: the cokernel of a map with generating image
items.statement: Let f : W_1 → W_2 be a morphism of BC's with W_2 a B^+_dR-Module whose image generates it as a B^+_dR-Module. Then coker(f), if nonzero, is of curvature > 0 and height < 0. One may assume f injective and not surjective; then W_1 = H^0(X,F_1), W_2 = H^0(X,F_2) with F_1, F_2 of vanishing H^1 and F_2 supported at ∞, and f induced by f_X : F_1 → F_2, which the generation hypothesis makes surjective and the injectivity makes H^0(X,ker f_X) = 0; vanishing of H^1(X,F_1) gives coker(f) ≅ H^1(X,ker f_X). Since F_1 is not torsion — else it would be supported at ∞, making W_1 a B^+_dR-module and f surjective — neither is ker f_X, and its H^0 being zero its slopes are < 0, whence the conclusion.
items.note: Announced in §1.3.1 as one of the two key inputs (with Lemma 5.17) that tell one what happens when the sequence of the fundamental diagram fails to be exact on the right.

items.name: Lemma 3.24: curvature ≤ 0 as an extension of a curvature-0 object
items.statement: For W ∈ BC the following are equivalent: (i) W is of curvature ≤ 0; (ii) there is an exact sequence (3.25) 0 → V → W → M → 0 with M of curvature 0 and V finite dimensional over Q_p. For (i)⇒(ii) one writes W = H^0(X,F_∞) ⊕ (⊕_{d_i/h_i≥0}U_{d_i/h_i}) and uses the sequences 0 → Q_p^{h_i} → U_{d_i/h_i} → B_{d_i} → 0, taking V = ⊕ Q_p^{h_i}; the converse is Corollary 3.19(ii).
items.note: Since ht(V) = dim_{Q_p}V and ht(M) = 0, (3.25) gives ht(W) = dim_{Q_p}V for W of curvature ≤ 0 — precisely what Proposition 3.27(i) categorifies.

items.name: The functor h(W) = Hom_VS(W,B_dR): a categorification of height
items.statement: For W a BC set h(W) := Hom_VS(W,B_dR), a B_dR-module, so that h is a contravariant functor from BC to B_dR-vector spaces. By the arguments in the proof of Corollary 3.18, h(W) ≅ colim_{k≥0}Hom_VS(W,t^{−k}B^+_dR) = Hom_VS(W,B^+_dR) ⊗_{B^+_dR} B_dR, and likewise Ext^1_VS(W,B_dR) ≅ colim_{k≥0}Ext^1_VS(W,t^{−k}B^+_dR).
items.note: Announced in §1.3.1 as the interpretation of ht(W) for a qBC as the rank of Hom_VS(W,B_dR); it is what survives when there is no Galois action, i.e. in Conjecture 1.8. The colimit description of Ext^1 is quoted from Anschütz–Le Bras.

items.name: Lemma 3.26: Ext^1_VS(W,B_dR) vanishes for curvature ≤ 0
items.statement: (i) If W is of curvature ≤ 0 then Ext^1_VS(W,B_dR) = 0. (ii) For an exact sequence 0 → W_1 → W → W_2 → 0 of BC's of curvature ≤ 0, the sequence 0 → h(W_2) → h(W) → h(W_1) → 0 is exact. (ii) follows from (i); and by (3.25) it suffices to prove (i) for an affine object and for Q_p. For Q_p one uses the surjectivity of B^+_dR/t^{m+1} → B^+_dR/t^m and Ext^1_VS(Q_p,V_1) = 0 by dévissage, then the colimit description. For W affine one reduces to V_1 and uses 0 → t^{−k}B^+_dR → t^{−k−1}B^+_dR → t^{−k−1}V_1 → 0 together with Hom_VS(V_1,B^+_dR) = 0: the first two terms of the resulting sequence are both B^+_dR/t, so the transition map on Ext^1 is zero.
items.note: Ext^1_VS(Q_p,V_1) = 0 is quoted from Le Bras.

items.name: Proposition 3.27: rk h(W) = ht(W)
items.statement: (i) If W is of curvature ≤ 0 then rk(h(W)) = ht(W). (ii) In general rk(h(W)) = ht(W) + rk(Ext^1_VS(W,B_dR)). For (i), Lemma 3.24 gives 0 → V → W → M → 0 with M affine, hence 0 → h(M) → h(W) → h(V) → Ext^1_VS(M,B_dR) with h(M) = 0 and the Ext term zero by Lemma 3.26, so rk(h(W)) = dim_{Q_p}V = ht(W). For (ii) one takes a presentation 0 → V → W′ → W → 0 with W′ an extension of V_d by a finite dimensional V′; since W′ is of curvature ≤ 0 its Ext^1 vanishes, and the resulting exact sequence gives rk(h(W)) = rk(h(V′)) − rk(h(V)) + rk(Ext^1_VS(W,B_dR)) with ht(W) = rk(h(V′)) − rk(h(V)).
items.note: The categorification of height; §1.3.1 lists it as a main ingredient of Proposition 7.10, and it is used in Proposition 5.18. Ranks are B_dR-module ranks.

items.name: Topological Vector Spaces
items.statement: The section opens by announcing the need to enlarge BC so as to allow extensions by arbitrary B_m-Modules, m ≥ 1. A Topological Vector Space is a functor W : Λ ↦ W(Λ) from sympathetic algebras to the left heart LH(C_{Q_p}) with the property that the image of Hom(Λ,Λ′) × B is bounded in W(Λ′) whenever B is bounded in W(Λ); a morphism is a natural transformation, and a sequence is exact precisely when it is exact in LH(C_{Q_p}) for every Λ. So a TVS is a VS with values in the left heart, subject only to the extra boundedness condition; no finiteness is imposed.

items.name: Remark 4.2: every BC is a TVS
items.statement: The boundedness condition of Definition 4.1 is automatic when W is a BC, as follows from the decomposition (3.14) or from the existence of a covering of W by a direct sum of universal covers of p-divisible groups, these having natural lattices functorial in Λ.

items.name: The model for LH(C_{Q_p}) and the notation Hom_TVS, Ext^i_TVS
items.statement: Following Schneiders, LH(C_{Q_p}) is represented as the localization of the full subcategory of the homotopy category of C_{Q_p}, consisting of complexes 0 → E_1 --δ_E--> E_0 → 0 with E_0 in degree 0 and δ_E a monomorphism, at the morphisms u : E → F whose square is bicartesian; in particular for E ∈ LH(C_{Q_p}) the algebraic quotient E_0/E_1 is well defined. Hom_TVS and Ext^i_TVS denote the Hom and Yoneda Ext groups in the category of Topological Vector Spaces.
items.note: This is the device that lets a pair (W_1 → W_2) be a single object of the left heart with a well-defined algebraic quotient; it is used throughout §§4.3–4.5.

items.name: B^+_dR-Modules and B^+_dR-Pairs
items.statement: (i) A B^+_dR-Module W is a VS for which there is a topological B^+_dR-module W killed by a power of t — hence a B_m-module for m large — with W(Λ) = B^+_dR(Λ) ⊗̂_{B^+_dR} W for all Λ, so that W(C) = W; morphisms are morphisms of TVS's that are B^+_dR(Λ)-linear for every Λ. (ii) A B^+_dR-Pair is a TVS (W_1,W_2) obtained by this base change from a pair of topological B_m-modules, that is from an injection W_1 → W_2 on C-points; both W_1 and W_2 are then B^+_dR-Modules, and morphisms are B^+_dR-linear morphisms of TVS's. There are natural maps Hom_{B^+_dR}(W,W′) → Hom_{B^+_dR}(W,W′) → Hom_TVS(W,W′) and likewise for Ext, which Theorem 4.30 shows to be isomorphisms when the objects are reasonable of the same type. The completed tensor product is defined as the quotient of B_m(Λ) ⊗̂_{Q_p} W by the closure of the subspace generated by the λa ⊗ w − a ⊗ λw; a Banach basis (e_i)_{i∈I} of Λ over C, necessarily countable, lifts to one of B_m(Λ) over B_m, giving B_m(Λ) ≅ ℓ^∞_0(I,B_m) and B_m(Λ) ⊗̂_{B_m} W ≅ ℓ^∞_0(I,W).
items.note: The torsion condition is imposed on the module, but no finiteness of length or rank — that relaxation is what the whole section is about. Three distinct Hom/Ext theories are in play from here on: over plain pairs, over Pairs, and over TVS’s.

items.name: qBC and its height
items.statement: (i) A qBC is a Topological Vector Space W admitting a filtration 0 ⊂ W_{>0} ⊂ W_{≥0} ⊂ W with W_{>0} a BC of curvature > 0, W_{=0} := W_{≥0}/W_{>0} a B^+_dR-Pair, and W_{<0} := W/W_{≥0} a BC of curvature < 0. (ii) A morphism of qBC's is a morphism of TVS's compatible with the filtrations and inducing a morphism of B^+_dR-Pairs on W_{=0}. (iii) The height is ht(W) := ht(W_{>0}) + ht(W_{<0}), and depends only on the isomorphism class.
items.note: The relaxation relative to a BC is precisely in the middle graded piece: for a BC the canonical filtration has the same shape with W_{=0} of curvature 0, i.e. a finite length B^+_dR-module, whereas a qBC allows an arbitrary Pair. Uniqueness of the filtration is not part of the definition but Proposition 4.26. The introduction uses this height in Theorem 1.12: a qBC attached to a finite dimensional Q_p-vector space has ht = dim_{Q_p}.

items.name: Curvature of a qBC
items.note: Note the shift of meaning relative to §3: for a qBC "curvature = 0" now means "is a B^+_dR-Pair", where for a BC it meant affine, i.e. a finite length B^+_dR-module.

items.name: Whether the qBC filtration splits
items.statement: It is conceivable that the filtration on a qBC splits and that a qBC can be written non-canonically as a direct sum of a BC and a B^+_dR-Pair, but proving this requires understanding Ext^2(Y,W) for Y a BC and W a B^+_dR-Module. Presumably this group vanishes — it does when W is of finite length — but that remains to be proved, and the authors note in a footnote that they will show in a sequel that the vanishing always holds, that it does not imply the direct sum decomposition but only that a qBC is an extension of a B^+_dR-Pair by a BC, and that it allows one to prove that qBC is an abelian category. The caution is justified by the pathology of the left heart recorded in Remark 4.8(ii): a strict extension of a Hausdorff W ∈ C_K by a finite dimensional V splits, but for W = (W_1 → W_2) ∈ LH(C_K) one has instead 0 → Hom(W,V) → Hom(W_2,V) → Hom(W_1,V) → Ext^1(W,V) → 0, and if W_1 is dense in W_2 then Hom(W,V) = 0 and Ext^1(W,V) = Hom(W_1,V)/Hom(W_2,V) — for K = Q_p, W_1 = LA(Z_p,Q_p), W_2 = C(Z_p,Q_p) and V = Q_p this is D(Z_p,Q_p)/Mes(Z_p,Q_p), a big space in which 0 is dense.
items.note: Explicitly not proved in this paper; deferred to a sequel. This is also why §4.5 contains no statement about kernels, cokernels or exactness for morphisms of qBC’s.

items.name: The group T_Λ and the characters attached to the perfectoid disc
items.statement: For Λ sympathetic write Λ{X}‾ for the sympathetic closure of Λ{X}, H_{Λ{X}} for Aut_cont(Λ{X}‾/Λ{X}), and T_Λ for Colmez's extension of O_Λ by H_{Λ{X}}: the continuous automorphisms τ of Λ{X}‾ restricting on Λ{X} to X ↦ X + x(τ) with x(τ) ∈ O_Λ, so that τ ↦ x(τ) is surjective with kernel H_{Λ{X}}. Fix α_C : C{X}‾ → C with α_C(X) = 0 and set f(τ) := α_C(τ(f)), so that X(τ) = x(τ) and f(0) = α_C(f). For α ∈ C with p^nα ∈ 2pO_C let E_α ∈ C{X}‾ be the unique p^n-th root of e^{p^nαX} with E_α(0) = 1; there is a character χ_α : T_C → C^* with τ(E_α) = χ_α(τ)E_α and an additive character ψ_α : H_{C{X}} → Q_p with χ_α(σ)^♭ = ε^{ψ_α(σ)}, and since χ_α is a character, ψ_α(τ^{-1}στ) = ψ_α(σ).
items.note: So T_Λ/H_{Λ{X}} = O_Λ, which is used repeatedly to make cocycles factor through O_Λ.

items.name: Lemma 4.9: the perfectoid cover of the unit disc
items.statement: O_C{X}[(E^{1/p^n} − 1)/p^{1/p^{n+1}} : n ∈ N] is integral over O_C{X} and perfectoid, i.e. x ↦ x^p is surjective modulo p^r for some r > 0. With Y_n = (E^{1/p^n} − 1)/p^{1/p^{n+1}}, expanding (p^{1/p}Y_0 + 1)^p = e^{pX} gives Y_0^p + p^{(p−1)/p}Y_0^{p−1} + ((p−1)/2)p^{(p−2)/p}Y_0^{p−2} + ⋯ + p^{1/p}Y_0 = (1/p)(e^{pX} − 1), so Y_0 is integral over O_C{X} and Y_0^p ≡ X mod p^{1/p}; the same computation from (p^{1/p^{n+1}}Y_n + 1)^p = p^{1/p^n}Y_{n−1} + 1 shows Y_n integral over O_C[Y_{n−1}] with Y_n^p ≡ Y_{n−1} mod p^{1/p}.
items.note: Here E is E_1. This is what makes the almost étale descent step of Proposition 4.10 available.

items.name: Proposition 4.10: Ext^1_TVS(V_1,V_1) ≅ C
items.statement: Let 0 → W_1 → E → W_2 → 0 be an exact sequence of TVS's with fixed isomorphisms W_1 ≅ V_1 and W_2 ≅ V_1, let v ∈ C and let h ∈ E(C{X}‾) lift vX. (i) There is λ_v ∈ C depending only on v, and g ∈ W_1(C{X}‾) with ‖g‖ ≤ p·sup_{τ∈T_C}‖τ(h) − h − h(τ)‖, such that ℓ = h − g satisfies (σ−1)ℓ = λ_vψ_1(σ) for all σ ∈ H_{C{X}}. (ii) There is λ_E ∈ C with λ_v = vλ_E for all v, and E ↦ λ_E induces an isomorphism Ext^1_TVS(V_1,V_1) ≅ C. The proof notes that σ ↦ (σ−1)h is a continuous 1-cocycle on H_{C{X}} with values in C{X}‾, that almost étale descent and decompletion give H^1(H_{C{X}},C{X}‾) ≅ C{X} with inverse λ ↦ λψ_1, and that ψ_1(τ^{-1}στ) = ψ_1(σ) makes λ_h invariant under translation by O_C, hence a constant. Surjectivity uses that Ext^1 is a module over End_TVS(V_1) = C and that λ_E = 1 for E = B_2, computed with ℓ := v̂·log[X^♭_1]; injectivity is completed in Remark 4.14.
items.note: The bound in the proof is printed as a supremum over τ ∈ T_C of a quantity ‖h_σ‖ depending on the free variable σ, where h_σ = (σ−1)h was defined only for σ ∈ H_{C{X}}; the statement takes a genuine supremum over T_C, of the different quantity ‖τ(h) − h − h(τ)‖.

items.name: Lemma 4.11: the cochain c_τ and the additive lifting
items.statement: With E, v, h, ℓ = h − g and λ_v as in Proposition 4.10(i), and α_Λ : Λ{X}‾ → Λ with α_Λ(X) = 0: (i) c_τ := (τ−1)ℓ − α_Λ(τ(ℓ)) lies in Λ{X} for all τ ∈ T_Λ, and c_τ = c_{στ} = c_{τσ} for σ ∈ H_{Λ{X}}. (ii) There is u ∈ C{X} such that ℓ_v := ℓ − u is an additive lifting of vX, i.e. α_Λ(τ_1τ_2(ℓ_v) − τ_1(ℓ_v) − τ_2(ℓ_v) + ℓ_v) = 0 for all τ_1, τ_2 ∈ T_Λ. For (i) one computes (σ−1)c_τ = λ_v(ψ_1(τ^{-1}στ) − ψ_1(σ)) = 0. Viewing c_τ as a function F(X,x(τ)) and using the uniqueness of the lifted automorphism, the 2-cocycle (4.12) c_{τ_1τ_2} − τ_1c_{τ_2} − c_{τ_1} = −α_Λ(τ_1τ_2(ℓ) − τ_1(ℓ) − τ_2(ℓ)) becomes f(Y_1,Y_2) = F(X,Y_1+Y_2) − F(X+Y_1,Y_2) − F(X,Y_1) satisfying the additive 2-cocycle condition, and Lemma 4.13 writes it as a coboundary.
items.note: The conclusion of the proof omits the "+ℓ_v" of the statement; the two agree because α_C(ℓ_v) = 0 for an additive ℓ_v, an identity used explicitly later in the proof of Proposition 4.27.

items.name: Lemma 4.13: a 2-cocycle on the additive disc is a coboundary, with bounded denominators
items.statement: If f ∈ O_C{Y,Z} satisfies f(Y,Z) − f(X+Y,Z) + f(X,Y+Z) − f(X,Y) = 0 then there is u ∈ p^{−1}O_C{X} with f(Y,Z) = u(Y+Z) − u(Y) − u(Z). Normalising f(0,0) = 0 and setting Y = 0 gives f(0,Z) = f(Y,0) = 0, so f(Y,Z) = Yf_1(Z) + Y^2f_2(Z) + ⋯; differentiating at Y = 0 forces u′ = f_1, and subtracting the coboundary leaves a cocycle whose expansion starts in Y^2, which an induction on the cocycle relation modulo (Y,Z)^{k+1} shows to vanish. For integrality, a_k = i!/(k(k−1)⋯(k−i+1))·b_{i,k−i} for any i ∈ {1,…,k−1}; taking i = 1 when (k,p) = 1 and i = p^r with r = v_p(k) otherwise gives a_k = u_kb_{i,k−i} with v_p(u_k) ∈ {0,−1}, and since the b_{i,j} lie in O_C and tend to 0, a_k ∈ p^{−1}O_C and a_k → 0.
items.note: The bounded denominators are exactly what is reused in the proof of Proposition 4.18. The printed final formula has b_{i,k−1} where the displayed general formula, and the argument, require b_{i,k−i}.

items.name: Rank of an additive element, and the end of the proof of Proposition 4.10
items.statement: The rank of an additive element ℓ is the rank of the Z_p-module {(σ−1)ℓ : σ ∈ H_{C{X}}}. The construction so far shows that vX ∈ W_2(C{X}‾), which has rank 0, admits an additive lifting ℓ_v in E(C{X}‾) of rank ≤ 1, of rank 0 exactly when λ_v = 0, which is the case if E is split. For the converse — hence for injectivity in Proposition 4.10(ii) — if v ≠ 0 and ℓ_v has rank 0, then x ↦ s_v(x) := (τ_{x/v} − 1)ℓ_v is well defined, depends only on x/v, lifts x, and gives a functorial splitting vO_Λ → E(Λ) extending by Q_p-linearity to W_2(Λ) → E(Λ); functoriality uses that a lifting of u : Λ → Λ′ to the sympathetic closures is unique up to H_{Λ{X}} and that every τ′ ∈ T_{Λ′} has a unique compatible τ ∈ T_Λ.
items.note: This remark is load-bearing: it completes Proposition 4.10(ii), and is reused verbatim, adapted to the setting of Proposition 4.18, in the proof of Proposition 4.27.

items.name: Remark 4.15: the normalisation ψ_1 and the pro-étale interpretation
items.statement: (i) Privileging ψ_1 can seem arbitrary, but ψ_α − αψ_1 is a coboundary in C{X}‾: there is an additive f_α ∈ C{X}‾ with (σ−1)f_α = ψ_α(σ) − αψ_1(σ), a consequence of Colmez's theorem. (ii) Sp(C{X}) is a K(π,1), being an affinoid, and C{X}‾ is the completion of a pro-étale perfectoid extension of C{X}, so almost étale descent gives H^1(H_{C{X}},C{X}‾) ≅ H^1_proét(Sp(C{X}),O) and the proof of Proposition 4.10 gives Ext^1_TVS(V_1,V_1) ≅ H^0(T_C,H^1_proét(Sp(C{X}),O)) ≅ H^0(T_C,C{X}) = C.
items.note: This is the perfectoid point of view of the section title, given as an interpretation of the proof rather than re-proved.

items.name: Reasonable topological C-vector spaces and the associated TVS
items.statement: A topological C-vector space is reasonable if it is a fréchet or a compact inductive limit of banachs, and is separable, i.e. contains a dense C-subspace of countable dimension. For W ∈ C_C one writes W := B_1 ⊗̂_C W for the functor Λ ↦ Λ ⊗̂_C W; as a TVS B_1 ≅ V_1, but the notation B_1 emphasises that it is also naturally a B^+_dR-Module.
items.note: Two conditions, one on the type and one on separability; separability is what makes Hahn–Banach available without assuming C spherically complete.

items.name: Remark 4.16: strict exactness is preserved
items.statement: If 0 → W_1 → W_2 → W_3 → 0 is a strict exact sequence of reasonable topological C-vector spaces then the induced sequence of TVS's is exact — it suffices that 0 → Λ ⊗̂_C W_1 → Λ ⊗̂_C W_2 → Λ ⊗̂_C W_3 → 0 be strictly exact in C_{Q_p} for sympathetic Λ, which holds because the W_* are reasonable and Λ is a banach.
items.note: This is where reasonableness is needed: exactness of TVS’s is defined Λ by Λ.

items.name: The pushout extension and Ext^1_{B^+_dR}(C,W) ≅ W
items.statement: For W ∈ C_C and w ∈ W one builds the pushout E_w of C by W from 0 → C --t--> B_2 → C → 0 along c ↦ cw, i.e. E_w = (B_2 ⊕ W)/{(c,cw)}; it is visibly a B^+_dR-module, and the construction gives an isomorphism W ≅ Ext^1_{B^+_dR}(C,W). The associated TVS extension comes from the pushout of 0 → B_1 --t--> B_2 → B_1 → 0.

items.name: Proposition 4.18: Hom and Ext^1 out of B_1 into a reasonable space
items.statement: For W ∈ C_C reasonable the natural maps W → Hom_{B^+_dR}(C,W) → Hom_TVS(B_1,W) and W → Ext^1_{B^+_dR}(C,W) → Ext^1_TVS(B_1,W) are isomorphisms. For Hom, given α : B_1 → W put w = α(1); for each λ ∈ W^* the composite λ∘α : B_1 → B_1 is multiplication by an element of C, which evaluating at 1 is λ(w), so α is a ↦ aw. For Ext^1, an extension is controlled by the class of the 1-cocycle σ ↦ (σ−1)h on H_{C{X}}, and since every step in the proof of Proposition 4.10, including Lemma 4.13, involves bounded denominators, that proof goes through with orthonormal bases for W a separable banach; the fréchet case follows by projective limits, the R^1lim vanishing by the topological Mittag-Leffler criterion, and the compact type case reduces to the banach case by Lemma 4.19.
items.note: The dual space must be large enough, which is why separability is built into "reasonable". The proof splits by type: banach, then fréchet, then compact type.

items.name: Lemma 4.19: a continuous cocycle of a profinite group lands in one step
items.statement: Let H be profinite and W = lim_→ W_n a compact inductive limit of C-banachs with H acting continuously by isometries. Then any continuous cocycle σ ↦ c_σ on H with values in W has c_σ ∈ W_{n_0} for all σ, for some n_0. The closure B_n in W of the unit ball of W_n is c-compact, so U_n := Σ_{i=0}^n p^{i−n}B_n is a closed subgroup with W = ∪_n U_n; H_n := {σ : c_σ ∈ U_n} is a closed subgroup by the cocycle condition and the isometry hypothesis, and H = ∪_n H_n, so by Baire some H_{n_1} has non-empty interior, hence is open and of finite index; taking n_0 ≥ n_1 with W_{n_0} containing the c_σ for a system of representatives, the cocycle relation gives the claim.

items.name: Reasonable B_m-modules
items.statement: B_m is naturally a banach algebra, with ring of integers the image of A_inf. A topological B_m-module is reasonable if it is a B_m-fréchet, i.e. its topology is defined by a countable family of norms of B_m-modules, or a c-compact inductive limit of B_m-banachs. For W such a module one writes W := B_m ⊗̂_{B_m} W for the functor Λ ↦ B_m(Λ) ⊗̂_{B_m} W. Correspondingly, if 0 → W_1 → W_2 → W_3 → 0 is a strict exact sequence of reasonable topological B_m-modules then the induced sequence of B_m-Modules is exact, by reduction to the case m = 1.
items.note: Separability is not restated at the B_m level. "Of the same type" later means: both B_m-fréchet, or both of compact type. The display in Remark 4.20 is printed with the indices W_1, W, W_2 where the sequence under discussion has W_1, W_2, W_3.

items.name: The pushout extension of B_d and Ext^1_{B^+_dR}(B_d,W) ≅ W/t^d
items.statement: For W a topological B_m-module and w ∈ W the pushout of 0 → B_m --t^d--> B_{m+d} → B_d → 0 along c ↦ cw gives E_w = (B_{m+d} ⊕ W)/{(t^dc,cw)}, a B^+_dR-module; the extension splits when w ∈ t^dW, and the construction gives W/t^d ≅ Ext^1_{B^+_dR}(B_d,W).

items.name: Proposition 4.22: Hom and Ext^1 out of B_d into a reasonable B_m-module
items.statement: For W a reasonable B_m-module the natural maps W[t^d] → Hom_{B^+_dR}(B_d,W) → Hom_TVS(B_d,W) and W/t^d → Ext^1_{B^+_dR}(B_d,W) → Ext^1_TVS(B_d,W) are isomorphisms, where W[t^i] is the t^i-torsion. One argues by dévissage, first on m using 0 → W[t] → W → W/W[t] → 0, whose outer terms are reasonable B_{m−1}-modules, then on d using 0 → B_1 --t^{d−1}--> B_d → B_{d−1} → 0; the case d = m = 1 is Proposition 4.18 with Remark 4.21, and each induction step compares the six-term exact sequences by the five lemma.
items.note: This is the computational engine of §§4.4–4.5.

items.name: Reasonable B^+_dR-Pairs of the same type
items.statement: A B^+_dR-Pair W = (W_1,W_2) is reasonable when both W_1 and W_2 are reasonable B^+_dR-Modules of the same type, i.e. both fréchets or both of compact type. A qBC is reasonable when W_{=0} is a reasonable B^+_dR-Pair.

items.name: Lemma 4.23: Hom out of B_d into a reasonable Pair
items.statement: For W = (W_1,W_2) a reasonable B^+_dR-Pair there is a natural isomorphism (W_2/W_1)[t^d] ≅ Hom_TVS(B_d,W). One compares three five-term exact sequences — the Ext_{B^+_dR}(B_d,−)-sequence of 0 → W_1 → W_2 → W_2/W_1 → 0 without topology, the same computed in the left heart of topological B^+_dR-modules, and the Hom_TVS/Ext^1_TVS sequence — in which all vertical arrows but the middle ones are isomorphisms by Proposition 4.22, and applies the five lemma.
items.note: So as far as Hom out of B_d is concerned, the C-points of a Pair are the algebraic quotient W_2/W_1.

items.name: Lemma 4.24: Hom and Ext^1 out of U_d
items.statement: (i) If W is a reasonable B^+_dR-Module with W = W(C) then Hom_TVS(U_d,W) ≅ W and Ext^1_TVS(U_d,W) = 0 for all d ∈ N. (ii) If W = (W_1,W_2) is a reasonable B^+_dR-Pair then Hom_TVS(U_d,W) ≅ W_2/W_1. For (i) choose m with t^mW = 0 and compare, along the injection U_d ↪ B_{m+d}, the Hom/Ext sequences of 0 → Q_pt^d → U_d → B_d → 0 and of 0 → t^dB_m → B_{d+m} → B_d → 0 with the sequence 0 → W[t^d] → W --t^d--> W → W/t^d → W → W; since Ext^1_TVS(Q_pt^d,W) = 0 and Hom_TVS(t^dB_m,W) → Hom_TVS(Q_pt^d,W) is an isomorphism, the connecting map is surjective and Ext^1_TVS(U_d,W) = 0, whence by the five lemma Hom_TVS(B_{d+m},W) ≅ Hom_TVS(U_d,W). Part (ii) follows from (i) and the Ext sequence.
items.note: The Ext^1 assertion of (i) is printed as an isomorphism onto W, whereas the proof establishes its vanishing — and (ii) follows from (i) only through that vanishing.

items.name: Proposition 4.25: no maps from positive curvature into a Pair
items.statement: If Y is a BC of curvature > 0 and W a reasonable B^+_dR-Pair then Hom_TVS(Y,W) = 0. By §3.2.8, Y is a direct sum of pieces B_d/Q_p^h and U_d/Q_pt_x^d with x ≠ ∞, so one may assume Y is one of them. For Y = B_d/Q_p^h it suffices that Hom_TVS(B_d,W) → Hom_TVS(Q_p^h,W) be injective, and Lemma 4.23 identifies the source with W(C)[t^d], which injects into W(C) = Hom_TVS(Q_p,W), a quotient of the target. For Y = U_d/Q_pt_x^d the induced map W → W is multiplication by t_x^d, an isomorphism since θ(t_x) ≠ 0.
items.note: This is what makes W_{>0} maximal.

items.name: Proposition 4.26: the filtration of a reasonable qBC is characterised by maximality
items.statement: Let W be a reasonable qBC, i.e. one with W_{=0} a reasonable B^+_dR-Pair. (i) W_{>0} is the largest sub-BC of W of curvature > 0. (ii) W_{<0} is the largest quotient-BC of W of curvature < 0. For (i), a BC Y ↪ W of curvature > 0 maps to zero in W_{<0} by Remark 3.6 and to zero in W_{=0} by Proposition 4.25, so lands in W_{>0}. For (ii), a surjection W → Y onto a BC of curvature < 0 kills W_{>0}, hence factors through W_{≤0}; writing W_{=0} = (W_1,W_2), the map Hom_TVS(W_{=0},Y) injects into Hom_TVS(W_2,Y), and a morphism as above kills every finite length sub-B^+_dR-Module of W_2, whose union is dense, so it is zero and W → Y factors through W_{<0}. Hence the filtration is uniquely determined.
items.note: This is the defining property of the qBC filtration announced in Remark 4.6(i), and what makes it functorial.

items.name: Proposition 4.27: Hom and Ext^1 agree over modules, Modules and TVS’s
items.statement: If W_1, W_2 are reasonable topological B_m-modules of the same type, the natural maps (4.28) Hom_{B^+_dR}(W_2,W_1) → Hom_{B^+_dR}(W_2,W_1) → Hom_TVS(W_2,W_1) and the corresponding maps on Ext^1 are isomorphisms. For Hom one must only check that a morphism α of TVS's is B^+_dR-linear: linearity is tested on finite rank submodules, a finite rank sub-B^+_dR-module of W_2 is B_{d_1}e_1 ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ B_{d_s}e_s, Proposition 4.22 makes the restriction linear, and density of B^+_dR(Λ) ⊗_{B^+_dR} W_2 in W_2(Λ) with continuity of α_Λ finishes. The Ext^1 statement is much more delicate: Proposition 4.22 makes W := W(C) a B^+_dR-module, giving a map Res_C : Ext^1_TVS(W_2,W_1) → Ext^1_{B^+_dR}(W_2,W_1) inverse to the natural one, hence surjectivity; for injectivity one must show that if W → W_2 admits a continuous B^+_dR-linear section then W splits. When W_1, W_2 are killed by t one considers the set ℓ(W_i) of additive elements of rank 0 in W_i(C{X}‾), identifies it with W_i for i = 1,2 through v ↦ Xv and ℓ ↦ ℓ(1) — every such ℓ factoring through T_C/H_{C{X}} = O_C — and shows ℓ(W) → ℓ(W_2) surjective by Remark 4.14 adapted to Proposition 4.18. Then ℓ(W) ≅ W, and since W(C{X}‾) is reasonable by Appendix A and ℓ(W) is closed in it, the open mapping theorem makes this a topological isomorphism; composing the section with its inverse gives a continuous v ↦ ℓ_v with ℓ_v(1) = v, a splitting ℓ(W) = ℓ(W_1) ⊕ ℓ(W_2) and a C-module structure c·ℓ_v = ℓ_{cv}. Finally, for an orthonormal basis (e_i) of O_Λ over O_C, every element of W_2(Λ) is uniquely Σ_i e_iv_i with v_i → 0, one checks ℓ_{v_i}(e_i) → 0, and s(Σ_i e_iv_i) := Σ_i ℓ_{v_i}(e_i) is independent of the basis and functorial in Λ. The general case follows by dévissage on m_1 then m_2.
items.note: "Of the same type" is used through Appendix A, which is what guarantees that the extension W(C{X}‾) is again reasonable. Res_C is a one-sided inverse; and in the last computation v_i is printed as a sum over i where the argument, and the display three lines later, require a sum over j.

items.name: Lemma 4.29: ℓ_v is an additive, C-linear function on O_Λ
items.statement: ℓ_v : O_Λ → W(Λ) is a continuous group morphism, and is C-linear in the sense that ℓ_v(cx) = (c·ℓ_v)(x) for c ∈ O_C and x ∈ O_Λ. For additivity, τ ↦ (τ−1)ι_Λ(ℓ_v) is a continuous 1-cocycle on T_Λ; extending a continuous α : Λ → C to α̃ : Λ{X}‾ → C{X}‾ with α̃(X) = X gives α̃((τ−1)ι_Λ(ℓ_v)) = ℓ_v(α(x(τ))), so (τ−1)ι_Λ(ℓ_v) − ℓ_v(x(τ)) is killed by every α̃ and vanishes, and the cocycle τ ↦ ℓ_v(x(τ)) is a group morphism since T_Λ acts trivially on W(Λ). For C-linearity, choose c̃ : Λ{X}‾ → Λ{X}‾ with c̃(X) = cX, well defined on ℓ_v up to H_{Λ{X}}; then x(c̃^{-1}τc̃) = cx(τ), so τ(c̃(ℓ_v)) = c̃(ℓ_v) + ℓ_v(cx(τ)), and for Λ = C the element c̃(ℓ_v) − ℓ_{cv} is T_C-invariant with α_C-value 0, hence zero.
items.note: Internal to the proof of Proposition 4.27; it converts the abstract additive element into a continuous C-semilinear family, which is then summed against an orthonormal basis. The C-linearity argument is carried out for c a unit, while the statement asserts it for all c ∈ O_C.

items.name: Theorem 4.30: Hom agrees over pairs, Pairs and TVS’s
items.statement: For W = (W_1,W_2) and W′ = (W′_1,W′_2) reasonable B^+_dR-Pairs of the same type, the natural maps Hom_{B^+_dR}(W,W′) → Hom_{B^+_dR}(W,W′) → Hom_TVS(W,W′) are isomorphisms. The short exact sequence 0 → W_1 → W_2 → W → 0 in LH(C_{Q_p}) identifies each Hom with the kernel of Hom(W_2,W′) → Hom(W_1,W′), which reduces the claim to the case of a reasonable B^+_dR-Module; there one compares the five-term Hom/Ext sequences over Pairs and over TVS's, all vertical maps but the middle one being isomorphisms by Proposition 4.27, and applies the five lemma.
items.note: This is the promised justification of the assertion in Definition 4.4 that the three Hom-theories agree for reasonable objects of the same type.

items.name: Corollary 4.31: a TVS morphism of qBC’s is a qBC morphism
items.statement: For a morphism W′ → W″ of TVS's between qBC's of the same type, W′_{>0} maps into W″_{>0}, W′_{≥0} into W″_{≥0}, and the induced map W′_{=0} → W″_{=0} is B^+_dR-linear. The first part is proved like Proposition 4.26 and the last follows from Theorem 4.30.
items.note: With Definition 4.5(ii) this says that for qBC’s of the same type the forgetful functor qBC → TVS is fully faithful — the qBC analogue of Fontaine’s full faithfulness Theorem 2.1. The hypothesis is printed as "of the same type", and should be read as "reasonable of the same type", both Theorem 4.30 and Proposition 4.26 requiring reasonableness.

items.name: Scope of §5 and its role in the C_st-conjecture
items.statement: The chapter studies filtered (ϕ,N,G_K)-modules over K or C and their relation to the categories of almost C-representations and of BC's, introducing acyclic modules as a generalization of weakly admissible ones: while the modules (H^i_HK(X_C),H^i_dR(X)) coming from algebraic geometry tend to be weakly admissible, those coming from overconvergent geometry tend to be only acyclic. Theorem 5.8 and its corollaries are used for the pro-étale-to-de Rham part of the C_st-conjecture over K, and Proposition 5.20 for the part over C. The two target formulas, stated in §1.3.2, are Hom_{G_K}((M ⊗_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r},B_dR) = M^*_K and Hom_VS((M ⊗_{F^nr} B^+_st)^{N=0,ϕ=p^r},B_dR) = M^* ⊗_{F^nr} B_dR for M of slopes ≤ r.

items.name: (ϕ,N)-modules and (ϕ,N,G_K)-modules, and their duals
items.statement: A (ϕ,N)-module over F or F^nr is a finite dimensional module M with a bijective Frobenius ϕ semilinear over the absolute Frobenius and a linear N with Nϕ = pϕN. A (ϕ,N,G_K)-module over F^nr is such a module with a smooth semilinear G_K-action commuting with ϕ and N, smooth meaning that the stabilizers of elements are open. The dual M^* is Hom(M,F) with ⟨ϕ(µ),v⟩ = ϕ(⟨µ,ϕ^{−1}(v)⟩), ⟨N(µ),v⟩ = −⟨µ,N(v)⟩ and ⟨σ(µ),v⟩ = σ(⟨µ,σ^{−1}(v)⟩); these operators again satisfy Nϕ = pϕN.
items.note: For a module over F^nr the dual must be read as Hom_{F^nr}(M,F^nr), which is what Corollary 5.9 uses.

items.name: Filtered modules over K and the dual filtration
items.statement: A filtered module (M,Fil^•) over K is a K-module with a descending filtration by sub-K-modules, exhaustive and separated. Its dual is M^* = Hom_K(M,K) with Fil^i_⊥M^* = (Fil^{1−i}M)^⊥. When the filtration is clear from the context it is omitted from the notation; thus the de Rham cohomology of a variety over K is a filtered module over K with the Hodge filtration taken for granted.

items.name: Filtered (ϕ,N)- and (ϕ,N,G_K)-modules over K
items.statement: A filtered (ϕ,N)-module over K is a (ϕ,N)-module M over F together with a filtration on M_K = M ⊗_F K; a filtered (ϕ,N,G_K)-module over K is a (ϕ,N,G_K)-module over F^nr together with a filtration on M_K = (M ⊗_{F^nr} K̄)^{G_K}. The dual is the dual (ϕ,N,G_K)-module with the dual filtration. Such an object is often written just M, or as a pair (M,M_K) as in the de Rham case: for X a smooth quasi-compact dagger variety over K, (H^i_HK(X_C),H^i_dR(X)) is a filtered (ϕ,N,G_K)-module over K by the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism.

items.name: Rank, degree, t_N and t_H; the Harder–Narasimhan ⊗-category
items.statement: The rank of a filtered (ϕ,N,G_K)-module over K is its dimension over F^nr. For rank 1 one chooses a basis e, writes ϕ(e) = λe and sets t_N(M) = v_p(λ), and lets t_H(M) = i for the unique i with e ∈ Fil^iM_K ∖ Fil^{i+1}M_K; for rank r one passes to det M = ∧^rM, so that t_N(M) = t_N(det M) and t_H(M) = t_H(det M) = Σ_i i·dim_K Fil^iM_K/Fil^{i+1}M_K. The degree is t_N(M) − t_H(M) as printed. Endowed with rank and degree, the category of filtered (ϕ,N,G_K)-modules over K is a Harder–Narasimhan ⊗-category in the sense of §3.2.2.
items.note: The printed sign appears to be the wrong way round; see the source issue recorded for it. Every use of the degree in §5 — Definition 5.1, Remark 5.2, and the proofs of Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4 — as well as the identification of the slope with that of the associated bundle in Remark 5.5(ii), requires deg = t_H − t_N. Definition 5.13, being stated directly on the bundle, is unaffected.

items.name: Weakly admissible and acyclic filtered (ϕ,N,G_K)-modules
